opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. Right now we have two very successful families of models. On one side, autoregressive transformers over discrete tokens, which have been incredibly powerful for language. On the other side, diffusion and flow-matching models, which work beautifully for continuous signals like images, video, and audio. And the world we want to model, especially if you care about physical AI, is fundamentally a mix of both. Language and symbols are discrete, but pixels, motion, and forces are continuous.

The current practice is mostly to bolt them together. You tokenize everything into discrete codes and run one big autoregressive model, or you keep a language model and attach a diffusion decoder to it. Both work to a degree, but each has a cost. When you quantize a continuous signal, you lose information and you put a lot of burden on the tokenizer. When you just glue two models together, the interface between them becomes a bottleneck, and the two parts don't really share their understanding of the world.

So I think the evolution will go toward a more unified formulation, where a single backbone can reason over both kinds of variables natively. Discrete parts may be predicted with something like next-token prediction, and continuous parts with something like a diffusion or flow objective, but inside the same model, sharing the same representation and attention. We're already seeing early versions of this, and I expect it to become much more principled.

A few things I think matter. First, good continuous tokenizers. Compressing video into a compact latent space, while keeping what's physically meaningful, is still a core problem. Second, scaling. We learned from language that simple objectives plus scale go very far, and the question is whether a hybrid objective scales just as cleanly. Third, efficiency. Video is enormous, and if we want models that think and act in real time, as a robot needs to, we need architectures that are far more compute-efficient than what we have now.

And longer term, I'm not even sure the discrete versus continuous split will stay as clean as it is today. Maybe we'll find one framework that treats discreteness as a special case of something continuous, or the other way around. My honest answer is that we're still early. But the direction is clear: one model that can perceive, reason, and generate across modalities, because that's what you need to build a real world model.

r001.rationale: It says a single backbone should handle both kinds of variables while sharing the same representation and attention.

r002.rationale: It speculates that one framework might treat discreteness as a special case of continuity, or vice versa, but does not suggest making the architecture entirely discrete or entirely continuous would simplify handling mixed signals.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That question sits right at the center of what we think about at NVIDIA with Cosmos, and honestly it's one of the open problems I find most exciting.

Let me start with why the split exists at all. Language is naturally discrete. Tokens, words, symbols. The transformer architecture and the whole LLM stack grew up around that, with next-token prediction and a softmax over a vocabulary. The physical world is not like that. Video, audio, robot joint angles, sensor readings, these are continuous signals. For a long time the two communities built fairly separate stacks: autoregressive models for discrete tokens, diffusion models for continuous data.

When we built the first Cosmos world foundation models, we actually released both flavors. An autoregressive version that tokenizes video into discrete codes, and a diffusion version that works in a continuous latent space. We did that partly because we didn't know which would win, and partly because they have different strengths. The autoregressive one is natural for streaming and for mixing with language. The diffusion one gives you much better visual fidelity and smoother dynamics. The discrete tokenizer throws away information. You can see it in fine textures and in subtle motion.

So how should the architecture evolve? My view is that we're converging toward a single backbone with modality-appropriate heads, rather than forcing everything into one representation. The transformer itself is agnostic. It's just attention over a sequence of vectors. What differs is the input embedding and the output objective. You can have a shared trunk that attends over text tokens and continuous video latents in the same context window, and then at the output you use a discrete prediction head for language and a flow-matching or diffusion head for the continuous parts. There's a lot of recent work in this direction, and I think it's the right direction.

The second piece is the tokenizer, or more broadly the encoder. I think people underestimate how much of the problem lives there. A good continuous tokenizer that compresses video aggressively, say by a factor of several hundred or a thousand, while keeping the semantics and the physics, makes the backbone's job dramatically easier. We spent a huge amount of effort on the Cosmos tokenizer for exactly that reason. The question of whether to quantize at the end becomes almost a detail if the encoder is good enough.

The third piece is the training objective, and this is where I'd say the field is still arguing. Next-token prediction gives you a very clean scaling story and very clean reasoning. Diffusion gives you a better model of high-dimensional continuous distributions. I expect we'll see hybrids become the norm, where the model reasons autoregressively in a coarse or semantic space and then decodes the continuous detail with an iterative refinement process. That's actually close to how you'd want a robot to think. Plan at the symbolic level, execute at the continuous level.

And the last thing I'd say, which is a bit of a bet, is that the real pressure to solve this won't come from chatbots. It will come from physical AI. A robot has to read a language instruction, watch a video stream, and output continuous motor commands, all in one loop, at real-time speed. You can't afford three separate models with glue code in between. That constraint is going to force the architecture to unify, and I think within a few years the discrete-versus-continuous question will feel like an implementation choice rather than a philosophical divide.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a shared backbone for text tokens and continuous video latents, but explicitly says not to force them into one representation and retains modality-specific heads. It does not clearly state that the signals share a common representation.

r002.rationale: The response favors a unified backbone with hybrid objectives. It does not suggest that making the architecture entirely discrete or entirely continuous would simplify handling mixed signal types.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to ask which representation is most natural for each part of the problem. Language has a very natural discrete representation. Images, video, and physical motion contain continuous structure, and forcing all of that into discrete tokens can introduce a bottleneck.

So I would expect an architecture that combines the two. You could have an autoregressive component for reasoning over discrete symbols and a continuous generative component for producing visual detail or motion. The important question is how tightly those components interact. If the discrete model makes a plan that the continuous model cannot execute, you want feedback between them, rather than just a one-way pipeline.

Ultimately, I think the goal should be a shared understanding across these signals, with different ways to represent and generate them. A unified model doesn’t necessarily need one identical mechanism for everything.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a shared understanding across signals, but says they may use different representations; it does not state that they share a common representation.

r002.rationale: The response favors combining discrete and continuous components and warns that forcing signals into discrete tokens can be a bottleneck. It does not suggest an entirely discrete or entirely continuous architecture would simplify mixed-signal handling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to recognize that discrete and continuous signals have different properties, so we shouldn’t necessarily force them into exactly the same representation. Language is naturally discrete, while images, audio, and physical motion have continuous structure. You want an architecture that respects those differences but allows information to flow between them.

One direction is to have specialized components for each modality, connected through a shared model. That model could use discrete representations for reasoning and planning, while continuous components handle perception and generation. The interesting question is where those interfaces should be, and how much of that structure the model can learn rather than having us specify it.

Ultimately, I would judge the architecture by whether those capabilities help each other. Can language guide precise visual generation? Can visual experience improve reasoning? That interaction is more important than simply putting every modality into one network.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a shared model with specialized discrete and continuous components, but says the signals need not use the same representation.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest making the architecture entirely discrete or entirely continuous to simplify mixed signals; it proposes components suited to each type.
